newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Seoul stocks end higher, Ssangyong shares rebound.
newsitem.headline: Seoul stocks end higher, Ssangyong shares rebound.

text.p: Seoul stocks closed higher on Thursday as two troubled carmakers went limit up and the securities watchdog vowed to crack down on corporate-related rumour mongering, brokers said.
The market welcomed the finance ministry announcement it would supply 1.5 trillion won to banks and merchant banks to ease tightening liquidity as a result of troubles with Kia.
The composite stock index rose 8.46 points to 739.04.
Ssangyong Group shares rebounded from their limit-lows, underpinned by a news report that a German auto giant would help finance Ssangyong Motors.
Ssangyong Motors and partner Daimler-Benz AG were said to be negotiating a capital increase by the German firm.
Kia Group said it was considering selling troubled Asia Motors.
Both Ssangyong and Asia Motors rose to their upper limits of 4,370 and 3,790 won respectively.
"The sharp rebound in the two ailing carmakers helped stabilise nervous investor sentiment," said Baik Doo-hyun at Hyundai Securities. "The market has now passed its critical momentum."

The Securities Supervisory Board said it started on Thursday cracking down on rumour mongers to protect investors and corporate activities. It said corporate-related rumours, which had subsided after the Hanbo and Jinro group crises, had increased after the Kia Group's troubles surfaced last week.
"This will prevent possible rumours that some another corporates are facing financial problems or will follow Kia's suit," said Park Jong-kwan at Coryo Securities.
Brokers said investors also had hopes of stabilising money market with falling interest rates. Yields on three-year corporate bonds fell three basis points to 12.10 percent.
Most Ssangyong Group shares rose. Ssangyong Paper rose to its upper limit to 17,300 and Ssangyong Oil gained 100 won to 16,400.
Kia Group shares were mixed with its flagship Kia Motors closing unchanged at 12,100 won. Kisan fell to yearly low of 5,110 won, while Kia Steel gained 160 won to 2,260.

"But there are still investor jitters lingering in the market. Unless there are clearer signs that those groups are safe, the market is unlikely to fully turn around," said Hwang Chang-joong at LG Securities.
Finance Minister Kang Kyong-shik was quoted by his officials as saying the government had no plans to intervene to save the struggling Kia Group.
"Nobody believes those companies will go bankrupt. But the problem is no one is able to find out what is really happening there and this has worried investors," said Park at Coryo.
Brokers said low-priced large-cap shares were in demand. LG Chemical hit new yearly high of 15,000 won with the day's heaviest trading volume of 1.63 million shares.
LG Electronics gained 400 won to 18,300 and Daewoo Electronics added 380 won to 8,450.
Negative ratings for Korean banks by Standard & Poors and Moody's Investors Service put a dent on banking shares but those shares rebounded to close up aided by broad-based buying interest.
The banking-sub index rose 3.54 points to 341.10, off the day's low of 331.48.
Brokers said many bank shares were trading at below par value of 5,000 won and said those shares had already reached their bottom level.
-- Yeom Yoon-jeong (822) 727 5647
